summary: Women's health research doesn't have enough data or funding. It also has a "leaky bucket" problem, according to Dr. Piraye Yurttas Beim, Founder and Chair of Eve's Ark. She says the limited resources that go into the field don't often turn into solutions that impact women's lives. That's why Eve's Ark is building Eve, the first digital matriarch and a transgenerational resource that only became possible with AI. Instead of asking every institution to pay for its own infrastructure, Eve's Ark built a shared digital foundation on AWS that grows with the work. "The women's health field lags behind other fields of medicine and biomedical research by decades, but in the era of AI we can catch up," says Dr. Beim. summary: The human brain is the substrate for every thought, movement, perception, and emotion we have. The person trusted to operate on it carries that responsibility into every decision — long hours in the OR, precision demanded at every turn. But too much of a clinician's day is still spent on everything around the care. From intraoperative judgment calls to the documentation and coordination that follow, that's the daily calculus for a neurosurgeon — and AI now has an opportunity to help with both. Healthcare is a multi-trillion dollar industry largely built on workflows designed decades ago. Data lives on different systems, on paper, or in a surgeon's head. The technology to capture clinical notes during surgery, interpret medical imaging, and forecast how a mass might evolve — that's not science fiction. It's possible. But possible and deployed are two very different things. In this episode, AWS's Randi Larsen sits down with Dr. Chetan Bettegowda, the Harvey Cushing Professor and Director of Neurosurgery at Johns Hopkins, and Dr. Diego Socolinsky, who leads generative AI for the Americas at AWS and has spent 25 years moving AI from research into production — including deep roots in medical imaging and computer vision. title: AI and the Holy Organ: Inside Neurosurgery at Johns Hopkins | Amazon Web Services

summary: Can you trust what your AI agent does? In this [DATE] episode of GenerAIly Speaking, hosts Jay Busch and Bharathi Srinivasan answer that question twice with live demos, once for an agent in software and once for an agent with arms, a camera and a voice. First, Raviteja Sunkavalli shows how to observe an AI agent from its first prototype through production with Amazon CloudWatch Omni. He traces and evaluates an agent in the IDE while he builds it, sends telemetry with Agent Observability (ADOT SDK), walks the application map, triggers a real failure live, follows it from metrics to traces to logs, and asks Omni to investigate in plain language. He closes the loop by adding the failing case to the evaluation dataset so it is caught before the next release. Next, Jeremy Wallace shows Rad, an agentic AI companion robot he built with Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock and AWS IoT Greengrass. A Strands agent runs inside ROS 2, reasons and sees with Amazon Bedrock, speaks with Amazon Polly, remembers people, and asks before it moves while a digital twin previews the motion. You also see how AWS IoT Greengrass deploys it to the robot with short-lived credentials, so no AWS keys live on the robot, and how an AI coding agent helped design everything from the code to the 3D-printed body. summary: As online parking infringement appeals increased, Warrnambool City Council faced a growing workload and a manual review process that contributed to turnaround times of around 75 days, close to the 90-day deadline. Working with Amazon Web Services and AWS Partner Symphony3, the council built an agentic AI solution that brings together ticket, parking, and case management data for officer review. The solution has reduced the time officers spend reviewing each appeal by around 80 percent, while residents receive decisions in 7 days compared with about 75 previously. Each recommendation is supported by an auditable record, and officers spend less time gathering information manually.
